choices.text: Give {him} leave, and thank {him} for the cushion

effects.log: You give {him} leave, and a letter for the other teacher, who owes you more than {he} will ever know. It is a good cushion. {He} will come back in a few centuries, and you will still be here. You have got rather good at that.

mem.note: gave me leave, and took the cushion

choices.text: Set a real problem on the table, with the Veil off

effects.log: {npc} looks at the problem. {He} looks at you. {He} sits down very slowly on the cushion. "How long?" {he} asks. You tell {him}. {He} studies with you for the next four centuries and is the better for it, and {he} never again brings you a gift without checking it first.

mem.note: let me bring them easy problems

events.text: {npc} worries about you. {He} has been up here long enough to see how the isles treat those who do not rise, and {he} has taken to finding you small posts. Now {he} has come with a jade slip: a friend of {his} needs someone to look after a very small pavilion on a very quiet isle. "No one would trouble you there," {he} says, with love. "You would be safe." {He} has already arranged the skiff.

choices.text: Go and see the pavilion, and thank {him}

effects.log: It is a very small pavilion, on a very quiet isle, and there is a good view from it. You find you do not mind. {npc} visits every decade to see that you are managing. You always are, and you keep the skiff tied up in the way {he} likes.

mem.note: took the post I found, and thanked me

choices.text: Tell {him}, and show {him}

effects.log: You take {his} hands and let the Veil fall, there among your own. {npc} stands very still in all that weight. "I arranged the skiff," {he} says at last, faintly, and then starts laughing and cannot stop. The whole family has heard by the next drift. It will be years before {he} forgives you, and {he} will enjoy every one of them.

mem.note: told me the truth at last, after I had arranged the skiff

events.text: Your pantheon holds its Counting at the turn of the age, and each god lays on the altar what they have gathered. The great ones bring storms and harvests. You bring what your Mask would bring: a damp handful of small prayers. The Pantheon's steward moves it to one side with a fingertip, and thanks you for coming, and asks if you have considered a smaller pantheon.
events.arc: The Mask of a Lesser God

choices.text: Take your handful home, and answer every one of them

effects.log: A lost goat. A sore tooth. A boy who wants the girl at the mill to look up. You see to them all, one by one, for a whole season. The great ones have not answered a sore tooth in ten thousand years, and it turns out those are the prayers that mean it.

choices.text: Lay it on the altar again, with the Mask off

effects.log: The altar cracks from end to end under a damp handful of prayers. The steward goes down on his face, and the storm gods stop their talking one by one. They give you a place on the high step, and they begin asking you what you want, very politely. Nobody prays to you about a tooth after that.

events.text: Your domain's lesser spirits have begun to go elsewhere. It is nothing personal. A river-sprite gave notice this morning, and she has been frank about it. "The neighbours are saying this domain has no real god in it," she says. "Only somebody minding it. I have a family to think of." Behind her is a line of hill-spirits with their bags packed, and a very small wind who has come to ask for a reference.
events.arc: The Mask of a Lesser God

choices.text: Write them all a good reference

effects.log: You write every one of them a good reference, the wind too. The domain is very quiet afterwards. It is yours and you can hear yourself in it, and in the spring some of them come back, and they do not say why, and you do not ask.

choices.text: Ask the sprite to look after the place, just until you find someone

ok.log: She stays a week, and then another, and she has never been given so much to do. By summer she is running the river, and her family has moved in, and the neighbours are hearing about it from her.

fail.log: She gives you a very kind look, and a very firm no. The wind stays, though. It has nowhere else to go.

choices.text: Take off the Mask, on your own ground

effects.log: Every stream in the domain stands up in its bed. The hill-spirits put down their bags, and then they put down their heads. No spirit will ever leave you again. No spirit will ever tell you anything frankly again either, and the river-sprite curtseys now, and you liked her better before.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has found you a place in its smallest office, the Bureau of Minor Apologies, and your superior there is a god of no great size who enjoys having one person smaller than himself. Each morning he reads your work aloud and sighs. This morning a warrant has come down that he has signed without reading, and it is wrong. A small god in the eastern hills is going to be sealed under a bell for it.
events.arc: The Mask of a Lesser God

choices.text: Say nothing, and quietly lose the warrant

effects.log: It takes you a month, and a good deal of misfiling. The small god in the eastern hills will never know how near it came. Your superior sighs over your filing, and reads it aloud, and you find you do not mind that at all.

choices.text: Bring him an apology to sign, addressed to the eastern hills

ok.log: He signs it, then stops, and reads it for the first time in his long service. The warrant is withdrawn on his own authority. He has never been so proud of himself, and you bring him his tea.

fail.log: He signs it unread, like all the others. Now you have to lose the warrant and the apology.

choices.text: Carry the warrant up to the Court yourself, with the Mask off

effects.log: The Bureau of Minor Apologies has never had so many visitors. The warrant burns where it lies, and the Court's own judges come down the stairs to ask what else they might have got wrong. Your superior will not meet your eye, and he reads nothing aloud any more. It is very quiet in there.

events.text: The sect you founded has followed you up into the Divine Realm, in a manner of speaking: a few old immortals, a few young gods, one isle moored at the edge of a domain. A messenger from the Elder Lineages has come to explain how things are done here. "A house of your size has a patron," she says, glancing at your Mask. "We would be happy to be yours. You will find the terms are all quite customary." The terms are nine scrolls long.
events.arc: The Mask of a Lesser God

choices.text: Read all nine scrolls, with care, and ask questions

effects.log: The questions take forty years. The messenger is replaced twice. Somewhere in the seventh scroll you find a clause that the Elder Lineages have forgotten about, and you make a small note of it, and you say nothing. Your people have never been so well protected or so bored.

choices.text: Hand back the scrolls, without the Mask

effects.log: The nine scrolls roll themselves shut. The messenger steps back and bows at the proper depth for the first time, and it takes her a moment to work out what that is. No patron will trouble your domain for an age. All your people stare at you when you walk by, and the old immortals who came up with you have a question or two.

events.text: The elders of your house have come before the tablets with their faces arranged. "There are gods who count the houses, and they have begun to count ours as vacant," the eldest says. "A house whose head wears a face like that one cannot hold what it holds. We would like you to think about the children." The children in question are several thousand years old, and they are listening behind the screen.
events.arc: The Mask of a Lesser God

choices.text: Call the children in, and ask what they would do

effects.log: It is a very long evening. Some of them are fools and one of them is not, and you had not known which. The gods who count the houses go on counting. You still have the seat, and now you know who should have it after you.

choices.text: Stand before the tablets, and take off the Mask

effects.log: The screen falls over, with several thousand years of children behind it. The tablets of your house blaze up, the oldest first, like a line of beacons along a coast. The gods who count the houses count again, and they send a very handsome apology. The elders have rearranged their faces. They do it very quickly, and you notice how practised they are.

events.text: The Rolls of the Divine Realm are read out once an age, and yours has been left until the end, with the gods of very small things. The reader reaches you, and pauses. "Is this one still with us?" she asks the hall. Someone says they think so. Someone else says they have seen you near a pond. You raise your hand, from the back, and the reader looks in your general direction and makes a small mark.
events.arc: The Mask of a Lesser God

choices.text: Go back to the pond

effects.log: It is a good pond. There is a heron. The Rolls will not be read again for an age, and nobody up there will think about you until then. You do not know of any other god who can say that, and you do not know of any who sleep so well.

choices.text: Stand up at the back, and take off the Mask

effects.log: The reader's scroll goes straight up in the air and stays there. All the gods of very small things turn round to stare, then all the rest. She reads your name again, with your true rung beside it, in a voice that shakes. At the pond the heron does not come back that year, and you had got used to it.

events.text: {npc} has served at your shrine for an age and {he} has come to a decision. A great god has offered {him} a place, and {he} is too loyal to take it without telling you. {He} kneels and tells you, and then {he} says the worst thing of all. "I will stay, if you need me to. I know how little you have." {He} means every word. There is a small, patched offering bowl in {his} hands, and {he} has been mending it for you.
events.arc: The Mask of a Lesser God

choices.text: Bless {him}, and send {him} to the great god

effects.log: You bless {him} with exactly as much light as your Mask allows, and it is not much. {He} weeps, and goes. You have also, in that small blessing, put something that will save {his} life one day, and you will never mention it. You mend the bowl yourself after that.

mem.note: blessed me and let me go, with so little

choices.text: Take the bowl from {him}, with the Mask off

effects.log: The patches on the bowl turn to gold where you touch it. {npc} looks up and goes white, and then {he} puts {his} forehead on the stone. "I offered to stay," {he} whispers, "out of pity." You say you know. You say it was the finest thing anyone has done for you in an age. {He} stays, and it is never quite so simple between you again.

mem.note: let me pity them, for an age

events.text: {npc} has been making excuses for you to the rest of the family for longer than most kingdoms last. {He} tells them you are resting, that you are between domains. Now {he} has come to your little shrine with a basket, and {he} is pretending to admire the jar. "It is a very good jar," {he} says. "You must come to the gathering. Nobody will ask you anything. I have told them not to." {He} has a smudge of soot on {his} cheek, from mending someone else's hearth to pay for what is in the basket.
events.arc: The Mask of a Lesser God

choices.text: Go to the gathering, and let {him} make your excuses

effects.log: You go. Nobody asks you anything, very loudly. {npc} sits next to you the whole evening, and passes you things. On the way home {he} takes your arm. It may be that {he} has always known, and it may be that {he} has not, and you find that you do not want to ask.

mem.note: came to the gathering, and let me make the excuses

choices.text: Wipe the soot off {his} cheek, and take off the Mask

effects.log: The jar on the shrine rings, and every hearth in the old house lights itself. {npc} stands with the basket, not moving. "I sold my good fire-tongs," {he} says at last, in a very small voice, "for that basket." Then {he} hits you, quite hard, and then {he} holds on to you. The family has a great many questions by morning.

mem.note: told me the truth at last, after I had sold my good fire-tongs

events.text: The hall you joined keeps a list on the door of who may eat at the upper table, and it goes by what the Hall-Warden feels when you walk in. These days he feels very little from you. "We will find you something useful," he says. He has found you the geese. Three newcomers have gone past you to the upper table since the thaw, and one of them is asking you to hold her coat.

choices.text: Hold the coat, and go and see to the geese

effects.log: They are terrible geese. They are also the only creatures in the hall who take no notice of the Hall-Warden, and you start to find that restful. You also hear a good deal, holding coats.

choices.text: Walk in by the upper door, without the seal

effects.log: The Hall-Warden drops his ladle in the soup. The whole hall stands, not from respect, not at first, but because their knees have heard something. Your name goes to the top of the door by nightfall. The newcomer takes back her coat herself, with both hands, and from then on nobody asks you to hold anything, ever.

events.text: You founded this hall in {pw_world} with your own two hands and a borrowed mule. Lately the village has started sending its children to the hall over the river instead, because that one has a real master. The carter says so to your face, quite kindly, as he delivers your reduced order of turnips. "You keep a very tidy yard," he adds. "Everyone says so."

choices.text: Sweep the yard, and teach the three who stayed

effects.log: Three is a good number. You can see all of what each of them does wrong. In ten years the village will be talking about those three, and it will never occur to anyone to ask who taught them. The yard is indeed very tidy.

choices.text: Hold an open day, and let the children try to knock over the mule

ok.log: They cannot, and it is a very funny afternoon, and by the end of it you have eleven new pupils who think it is all about the mule. It is, in a way.

fail.log: They knock over the mule. It is a bad afternoon for the mule, and for your reputation.

choices.text: Go down to the river, and let the seal go on the bank

effects.log: The river stops talking. On the far bank the real master comes out of his hall and stands there for a long moment, then bows, deeply, across the water. Every child in the village is at your gate by morning, along with their parents, and they all want something. You will not have time to sweep the yard again.

events.text: You were born to one of the Old Houses, or a small corner of one, and at the Reckoning of Names each branch has its members read out, in order of what they are worth. You come after the dogs. It is a joke, your cousin says, and everyone laughs, and it was his joke last year as well. Your great-aunt has saved you a seat near the door, where you will not be in anyone's way.

choices.text: Take the seat by the door, and scratch the dogs

effects.log: They are very good dogs. You get to know them, and your great-aunt, who it turns out knows where every coin in the House has gone for the last sixty years. She thinks you are harmless, so she tells you.

choices.text: Read your own name out, and let the seal go

effects.log: The hall falls silent, and all the dogs lie down. You say your name, once, and it carries to the far end. Your cousin's joke does not get told again, by anyone. They move you up the table at once, and they do it with such speed that your great-aunt has to be helped out of the way, and she does not forget it.

events.text: The elders of your house have walked up from the valley together, which they only do for funerals and for this. "We are not saying anything," the eldest begins. "But the other Houses are saying it. They ask who it is that holds the name, and whether a person who barely stirs the dust can hold a wall when the raiders come." They all look at the wall. It is a very old wall, and it wants mending.

choices.text: Hand them each a trowel

effects.log: They are outraged, then embarrassed, and then they are mending the wall. You work beside them until dark. Nobody says anything further, and there is a great deal to be said for an elder who is too tired to talk. The other Houses go on saying it, and it does no harm.

choices.text: Put your hand on the wall, and let the seal go

effects.log: The old wall settles with a long groan, every stone of it going home, and it will not want mending again in your lifetime. The elders stand there with their mouths open. The other Houses hear it by market day, and they stop saying anything at all. Your own people have started to take off their hats to you, and the eldest no longer tells you when you are wrong.

events.text: The name of your line has gone back a long way in {pw_world}, and the singers keep it. Now the old singer of your house has come to ask, with great delicacy, what he should put in for you. He has a verse for every head who ever lived. "It need not be long," he says. "A line. Something about your good health. We could perhaps mention the weather, in your time, which was fair."

choices.text: Tell him the weather will do nicely

effects.log: He is very relieved. So you go into the song as a line about fair weather, between two long verses about wars. Children will skip that part. In a hundred years it will be the only verse with nobody dead in it, and you are not unhappy about that.

choices.text: Sing him the verse yourself, without the seal

effects.log: You have no voice to speak of. It does not matter. The whole house hums along, the rafters and the pots, and the old singer's harp sounds by itself. He writes it all down with his hand shaking. All your line stands taller for it, and from now on every heir will be measured against it, and you have made sure they will all come up short.

events.text: The small kings of {pw_world} send one another gifts at midwinter, and the gifts are a kind of language. This year the King of the Far Marches has sent you a very old and gentle pony, the sort one gives to a child or a grandparent. Your whole hall has seen it. Your chief counsellor clears her throat, then points out, without looking at you, that the King has been buying a lot of iron.

choices.text: Thank him warmly, and ride the pony to the next assembly

effects.log: You look absurd, and you ride it slowly, and you get a good long look at his iron on the way. Your counsellor has stopped clearing her throat, as she has started to see what you are up to. The pony is, in fact, a very nice pony.

choices.text: Send him a very small and exact pair of iron horseshoes, with a price

ok.log: They are made from his own iron, bought through three of his own merchants, and the price is what he paid for it. The Far Marches take a long look at that, and there is no war this year.

fail.log: He has them mounted on the wall, and sends a thank-you note. His smiths go on working.

choices.text: Ride to the assembly, and let the seal go in front of the kings

effects.log: The pony does not mind at all. Everything else does. Banners go flat, horses kneel, and the small kings of {pw_world} look at one another and then at the ground. There is no iron bought for a generation. Your counsellor no longer clears her throat, and you have begun to wonder what she is not saying.

events.text: {npc} has started doing the hard parts of the lessons for you, without being asked. {He} stands in front of you when the village lads come to jeer, and {he} has told them you hurt your back. This evening you catch {him} rubbing liniment into a bad shoulder, got in a scuffle that {he} has not mentioned, on your account. "It is nothing," {he} says. "You have given me everything. It is my turn now."

choices.text: Say thank you, and fetch more liniment

effects.log: You rub it in yourself. It is a very bad shoulder, and you know exactly how to fix it, and you do so while pretending to know nothing about it. The lads stop jeering around then, for some reason. {npc} thinks {he} did that, and {he} walks taller, and you let {him}.

mem.note: let me stand in front of them

choices.text: Go down to the lads yourself, with the seal off

effects.log: It takes no time at all. The lads are gone over the hill, and they are still running at the river. {npc} stands in the yard, one hand on {his} shoulder. "You let me," {he} says. "All that time." You say yes. {He} goes in and shuts the door, and in the morning there is breakfast, as always, and {he} does not meet your eye.

mem.note: let me take the blows for them

events.text: At the family's table in {pw_world} you are the one they worry about. {npc} has brought somebody along to dinner who needs a hand with some sheep, and {he} has told them that you are very reliable. It is a kind thought. {He} gives you a look over the bread, a long one, and you wonder about it. Last week you picked up the end of the cart with one hand and forgot that anyone could see you.

choices.text: Agree to help with the sheep

effects.log: You do. They are very good sheep. {npc} walks you to the gate after, and {he} looks at the cart, and then at you, and {he} says "Mind your back," in a voice that could mean anything. You do not ask. You mind your back.

mem.note: helped with the sheep, and minded their back

choices.text: Lift the whole table, with the bread on it, and tell {him}

effects.log: The bread does not even slide. You set it down again and let everything go at once, and all the cups in the house ring. {npc} goes on chewing for a while. "I knew about the cart," {he} says. Then {he} starts shouting, and it is about all the years {he} has been lifting things for you. It goes on until morning, and it is one of the best nights of your life.

mem.note: told me the truth at last, over the bread
